utterances.text: Well, the substantive difference was who this referred to. It actually referred to all members of the service except for those who were on combat duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these rules on disciplinary responsibility during a state of war shortened the proceedings, disciplinary proceedings, or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any details, but I know that there were disciplinary commissions and there was a prescribed procedure as to who starts the initiative and the procedure, and there was a possibility to appeal such a decision and that was the ministry itself or the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, tell us, can you remember approximately how many disciplinary proceedings you had against members of the MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I really cannot remember but I know that there were such cases. However, I cannot recall an actual number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the most serious punishment was in such cases of disciplinary infractions by members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dismissal from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what is the purpose of tendering this document? It's about a traffic accident so it's not for the purpose of the disciplinary fact, the fact committed. What is the purpose of tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was considered as a breach of disciplinary responsibility. I'm not offering it to show which breach it was, I'm just showing it that the CSB was conducting this disciplinary, or actually, disciplinary proceedings and giving disciplinary measures to the -- it's members in 1992 contrary to what the opposing party's theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, we say no disciplinary measures for serious offences such as murder, beating in prisons, and like this. I'm perfectly happy to accept; traffic accident, disciplinary proceedings taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it doesn't advance the issues before us any, so we don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Bjelosevic, during your testimony we discussed the situation in the -- or rather the public security station of Doboj. In the public security station of Doboj were there any omissions in their work in your view?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please remind us who the chief of the public security station of Doboj was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Obren Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take disciplinary measures against Obren Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If necessary, I can explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these documents you could see that there was a continuity involved in terms of these omissions in work, these omissions were pointed out. I had discussions with the then chief of the station, Petrovic, since the situation was changing slowly, we saw from documents that there were even obstructions in terms of carrying out orders and instructions. I finally suggested to the minister that Obren Petrovic be replaced and dismissed from this position of chief of the public security station. I think it was the beginning of 1993 when a new chief of the public security station of Doboj was appointed, Mr. Milorad Novakovic. When Obren Petrovic left the service, he did not wait for a new appointment decision so his departure actually pre-empted my intention of carrying out disciplinary proceedings because we were collecting evidence at that point in time for initiating disciplinary proceedings against him. Since he had left the service as such, these proceedings were never carried out in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in relation to Mr. Savic - you told us about him on the second day of your testimony here - did you establish in his case was that there were omissions in his work?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were omissions. When we talk about Milan Savic, I had in mind the results of the work of the team that investigated the situation in Teslic. I had in mind who was included in the criminal report and who was not. Since Milan Savic was not on the list of persons against whom criminal proceedings were instigated, and I was not able to automatically instigate proceedings against him, I continued to gather evidence about his omissions step by step, slowly, and when I wanted to instigate disciplinary proceedings, Milan Savic left the service. He was appointed the manager of ZOIL it's an insurance company. No, excuse me, it was Omnikom. He was appointed for the manager of Omnikom and Obren was appointed to a managerial position in ZOIL. So Milan Savic left the service and continued working as a manager in Omnikom and Obren Petrovic was appointed a manager in ZOIL.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, we saw that those men left the Ministry of the Interior. How did that affect their disciplinary responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the rules and the law, you cannot conduct disciplinary proceedings against somebody who is not in the service. The rules pertain only to the persons employed in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the fact that they left the service, that they did not work in the Ministry of the Interior anymore, did that affect their criminal responsibility in any way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Criminal responsibility is something different. Criminal responsibility is ascribed to any perpetrator of criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that also go for the members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in 1992 do you remember whether in the security services centre there were disciplinary proceedings against members of the Ministry of Interior for grave breaches of their duties related to, let me put it this way, mistreatment of non-Serbs or something similar?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically whether something was related to that, but there were disciplinary proceedings. I think that there were some cases related to the treatment of the persons of Muslim ethnicity. I wouldn't want to make a mistake here. I think that one of the inspectors was involved in something like and I think that there were disciplinary proceedings against him, but I really can't remember now without refreshing my memory through documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 281D1, tab 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, could you remind us, who was Veljko Solaja and what was he doing in the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Solaja was an inspector in the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 15th of December, 1992. It's signed by chief of centre Andrija Bjelosevic and it's about a complaint filed by Veljko Solaja on termination of his employment. It was sent to the minister together with the whole case file is so that the minister could make a decision on appeal. Is this your document and do you remember details of the case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a cover letter that went together with the disciplinary case against inspector Veljko Solaja. He was imposed a disciplinary measure of termination of employment. He was an inspector and I think it may have been connected to what I mentioned just a moment ago, certain acts towards individuals of Muslim ethnicity. And then Mr. Solaja appealed the disciplinary measure that had been imposed on him, and then in accordance with the rules, the whole case file together with this cover letter was sent to the ministry, or more precisely, the minister, at the appeals level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the outcome of this appeal was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really can't remember the outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. I think it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but it may be relevant especially if we could shed some light over what exactly had Mr. Solaja done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I was going to ask just that, where is the rest of the document. The file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor. This is just one page, and if the Prosecutor has the whole file, I would be more than happy to introduce the whole file. I just have this one document which was disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I am sorry, Your Honours, that may well have been disclosed to you by the Office of the Prosecutor. We disclosed what we had. If we had the file, no doubt we would, but the bulk of the documents that Mr. Bjelosevic have been going through have been provided by him. Did he provide the Defence with the rest of the file?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document, Your Honours, this document is batch 170 disclosure by the Office of the Prosecutor document 198.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Court order, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any interpretation or am I not supposed to hear anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You can listen to this, but the issue is not whether this document was or was not disclosed. The issue is what had Mr. Solaja done, what were the acts for which he was prosecuted or investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have asked the witness and maybe the witness can provide additional answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably didn't hear the question because you didn't hear interpretation. His Honour Judge Harhoff asked whether you could say something more specific about the reasons because of which the termination of employment was the disciplinary measure imposed on Veljko Solaja. What exactly did he do and how was it qualified?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm going to make a mistake. I think that I can remember that it was about taking money from individuals of Muslim ethnicity. I'm not sure but I think that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My reservation about admitting this is that it's the cover, and as Ms. Korner has pointed out, without the rest of the file, I don't see how it assists in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, simply this document shows that the -- that the CSB was conducting disciplinary proceedings against its members, the Serb members, for committing disciplinary whatever, mistakes or concerning the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, that's the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness says "I think." Your Honours, I certainly say that without the rest of the file this document is valueless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I find this, Your Honours -- I'm gravely concerned because I find this very unfair. We have admitted during the Office of the Prosecutor case a number of documents which have not been complete documents, a number, and the explanation given is that this is all we got, we found. Now, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you, Mr. Zecevic, to say that of course each ruling that the Chamber makes is based on the particular document that is before it. The problem, as I see it, with this document is that, and I suppose it is because it was merely a cover forwarding certain other documents, is that standing by itself, and as Ms. Korner has pointed out, the witness has not been able to assist by expanding on it, it really says nothing. That's the practical question that I have. And we have the witness's testimony. This document adds nothing to what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I suggest that this document be MFI'd and that we try to locate the missing files. Maybe -- I'm very sure that there might be some way that our friends in the Office of the Prosecutor check their records again and maybe we'll be able to find some additional documents from this file. So therefore, may we have it MFI'd just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We could do that. So the document is marked for identification pending the completion of, for want of a better word, of the document. Discovery, thank you, the discovery of the report which comprises the remainder of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've checked our records on this and with the caveat that we don't always have everything completely recorded, the particular entry doesn't show that we have the file only as Mr. Zecevic points out, the cover letter. So we can't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in as much as the trial -- this trial isn't going to end tomorrow, we will see where we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, document number will be Exhibit 1D--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I could be of help. I am sure that it was an unlawful act of Veljko Solaja against persons of Muslim ethnicity. I'm one hundred per cent sure about that, but I can't remember what exactly it was that he did to them. That I cannot claim because I don't know that. But I'm sure that it was something in relation to individuals of Muslim ethnicity. I just don't remember exactly what act it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe we can deal with this after the break and can we just have, for the record, the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number is Exhibit 1D530 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered in, may I use the opportunity to give one additional important argument why I think that go in favour for admittance of these documents to the record, to exhibits. Your Honours, despite the nature of the breach of the disciplinary proceedings which are happening, despite whatever is the breach, it directly goes to the knowledge of the minister if he receives an appeal, it goes to his knowledge and this document shows he received an appeal, that's beyond doubt. So it shows the knowledge of the minister that there exists a system, a disciplinary system and it's functional in the territory at the time. Therefore, therefore, Your Honours, this document is important for the knowledge of the ministry and the minister that the disciplinary system exists at the time: It -- of course it would have been better, I agree, that if we have the whole file, but still, the document on its own showing that the appeals and the minister receives the appeal, he can only conclude that the disciplinary system as provided by the law and the regulation is existing and functioning and therefore that is important for the aspect of knowledge of the minister. And relevant for this case definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that's the only matter for which its sought to be tendered and not sought to be tendered as evidence of disciplinary proceedings being taken against a Serb police officer in respect of crimes committed against a non-Serb, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I believe where we are is that this had been exhibited but the qualification was only marked for identification. By majority, Judge Harhoff dissenting, we would remove the MFI qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would the Trial Chamber expect me to pursue the last answer of the witness concerning this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought he had answered as best he could, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was my opinion also but I am in the hand of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, could you please be shown P855, tab 299. Tab 229.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have it on the screen. The document is only one page long. It will be enough for you to see it on the screen. This document was issued by the Ministry of the Interior. It's a dispatch dated 16 December 1992. The signatory is Minister Mico Stanisic, it says that it was sent to all chiefs of MUP administration, all chiefs of CSBs, did you receive this dispatch? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what the dispatch is about and did you act in accordance with it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch concerns suspension of individuals. If they are suspended, they should be placed at the disposal of the local command of the Republika Srpska Army without awaiting the results of disciplinary procedures. That was a very harsh measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we clarify one thing. The measure called suspension, when was it applied? At what moment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The measure of suspension was mandatory in case criminal proceedings were instituted against a MUP employee. In that case, we were duty-bound to act in keeping with this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did that measure suspension apply when disciplinary proceedings were instituted for serious breaches of duties?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this applied to the serious breaches, not to the lighter kind of breaches of discipline and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How should I understand the answer that you just provided, the two last answers. Did you say that suspension as a measure was applied both when criminal proceedings were instituted as well as when a disciplinary procedure was instituted for the grave breach of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both. It was mandatory if criminal proceedings were instituted as well as in cases when a disciplinary procedure was instituted for major breaches of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Witness. I don't have any more questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, could I just follow up on Counsel Zecevic's questions and ask you how exactly did this work in practice. If, say, one of your police officers had been engaged in activity and for that reason was subject to either criminal proceedings or disciplinary proceedings, would you then suspend the officer immediately or would you postpone your suspension until such time as the officer in question could in fact be resubordinated to the army? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were indications and indicia that a crime was committed and that criminal proceedings were to be instituted against an authorised official, a suspension was automatic. That person would be immediately suspended. The measure would also be applied if an authorised official violated his duties and that was prescribed by the regulations on disciplinary responsibility. In other words, the regulations stipulated what were minor breaches of discipline as opposed to major breaches of discipline. If a disciplinary procedure was started because of a major breach of discipline, suspension was a mandatory measure that was applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if I take it that it was then applied also immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But tell us then how was the re-subordination to the army then arranged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A suspended official was reported to the Ministry of Defence, a report would go to the Ministry of Defence about such individuals. The Ministry of Defence kept records on conscripts. The report would also state that that person was no longer an employee of the Ministry of the Interior and that the person was placed at their a disposal. Then the Ministry of Defence and its departments in keeping with the rules and regulations and in keeping with the requirements of war units would send such a person to any of the war units that had requested reinforcement in manpower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it would be the Ministry of Defence's duty to then assign the suspended officer to one of the units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. And that depended on the requirements of the units and priorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was the suspension of a temporary nature or was it permanent so to say until it was brought to an end by the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suspension was always temporary in nature, as it were. When criminal proceedings were completed, the person may be acquitted or convicted and in keeping with that such a suspended person is entitled to some other rights. And the same goes for disciplinary procedures. It doesn't necessarily mean that every disciplinary procedure will result in sanctioning the person who was subject to the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, when you ordered a suspension of one of your officers, the suspension would be in effect running until such time as the criminal or disciplinary procedures against him had been completed and by then he would come back to you; is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That could also happen but it depended on the outcome of the disciplinary procedure. One of the measures resulting from disciplinary proceedings may be the termination of employment which would just continue what was started with suspension. In case of a more lenient measure, the person who had been subject to the disciplinary procedure and was also suspended could claim certain rights, one of them being reinstatement in their previous position or monetary compensation, things like that. It all depended on the final outcome of either the criminal proceedings or the disciplinary procedure instituted against the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you have any influence over which part of the army your officer would be assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the officer continue to be paid, receive his salary from you or would he receive his salary from the Ministry of Defence while he was suspended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the moment of suspension his salaries and other benefits would arise from his further assignments. If he was assigned to a war unit, he would enjoy the same benefit as the other members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But on whose budget? Would it be the MUP budget or it be the Ministry of Defence budget?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would certainly not have been the MUP. I don't know how the Ministry of Defence funded the military. Different regulations regulated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One last question. Are you able to indicate just roughly how many of the police officers that were suspended under your authority did actually go to the front line? Was it all of them or half of them or somewhere between?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Defence assigned them from then on and I don't know how they did that. Our obligation was to hand them over and put them at the disposal of the Ministry of Defence. We were supposed to inform them that as of that moment they were no longer employees of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my question was really whether you kept track of them while they were suspended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, I have a couple of follow-up questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, one question. Let's imagine the following situation: A member of the MUP for the reasons that we have just discussed was handed over to the Ministry of Defence. Would that have been the case of re-subordination or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a completely different status. Re-subordination in legal terms was something else. In your imaginary case, the employee was no longer an employee of the MUP. He was given a new status by the Ministry of Defence and that had nothing to do with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelosevic, in case criminal proceedings were instituted against such an employee of the Ministry of the Interior would that person's removal from the records of the MUP and transferred on to the records of the Ministry of Defence, would that have had any influence on the course of the criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see why that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bjelosevic, if an employee of the Ministry of the Interior against whom a criminal proceedings were instituted was suspended and subject to criminal proceedings and he is remanded in custody, for example, would the -- his transfer or referral to the Ministry of Defence mean that he was released from custody or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was within the authority of the Court. The Court would decide whether they would be reminded in custody for any longer, whether they would be released. That had nothing to do with either the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now my last question: To His Honour Judge Harhoff's question, you explained what suspension was, that it was temporary, and how long it lasted. Based on the document that I showed you, P855, I believe that you still have it on the screen, the date is 16 December 1992. What effect does this minister order have on the suspension measure?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this order, would you say that the measure of suspension still had a temporary nature or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was still temporary in nature. If the outcome of the criminal proceedings was acquittal, then the suspended employee had all the rights and he can claim them if he wants to do so. Because his responsibility for the crime in question was not established so he was acquitted. And the same was true of disciplinary procedures. If the outcome a disciplinary procedure was acquittal and no charges were proven, then of course that person could exercise all of their rights, either the return to service or claiming benefits and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am asking you about this very specific document. How do you understand the order pursuant to which upon suspension every MUP employee temporarily removed from his tasks and duties is to be placed at the disposal the local responsible command of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be placed at the disposal of the army is one thing and this was done by the Ministry of Defence. The second issue is the criminal proceedings or the disciplinary procedure instituted against the person. Depending on the outcome of either of the two which could be either acquittal in which case the first case scenario would be for him to sue the authorities that charged him with the non-existent responsibility, but that did not leave any room for the person to wait in an undefined status. It was his obligation to report immediately to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the document we have on the screen, is that part of your list? I am a little bit at a loss. What tab number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is tab number 229 and this is Exhibit P855. Office of the Prosecutor 65 ter 2675. And it's been exhibited and is now Exhibit P855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon once again, Mr. Bjelosevic. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm a Defence counsel for Stojan Zupljanin. We met briefly before you started testifying. I'm going to put some questions to you today that have something to do with what you said here in court. I'm also going to ask you about certain things that you did not refer to here in court but you did in your interview with the OTP. The OTP disclosed certain documents to us as a later stage so I didn't manage to go through these documents with you, but you are basically familiar with these documents so we will be able to understand each other. Mr. Bjelosevic, when answering the questions of the Prosecutor in your interview from 2004 and 2009, you spoke about a few meetings you had with Stojan Zupljanin, so my questions will have to do with that. First of all, on page 51 of this interview, that is for the Prosecutors and the Trial Chamber to know what this is about, it's 2004. You mentioned meetings with Saric from Tuzla in December and you mentioned meetings with Stojan Zupljanin in 1991, 1992. That's the period. And then you say when answering the Prosecutor's question in terms of what it was that you discussed with Zupljanin, you said that you had similar problems --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I am afraid that the page numbering is separate for each of the tapes in the first interview, so if you could possibly tell me which tape it is. And secondly, I'm sorry, Mr. Krgovic, but you are going very fast and the interpreter is somewhat behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. T-002550 to T-002533 that's in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said then that when you talked to Mr. Zupljanin, you had similar problem, problems similar to the ones you discussed today. You said that that means that the top people of the municipal public security stations had turned to the Crisis Staffs and municipal leaders, municipal officials, there was a lack of co-operation on the part of the police to carry out their police duties. There were problems with supplies and similar problems with some criminal groups that were in your area and the area of Mr. Zupljanin. Basically, that you had to face similar problems; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as motivation is concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Krgovic please turn off his microphone, we cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there were indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many people who were exceptionally good policemen before the war and in that pre-war period they wanted to work in a way in which they were used to work, and they were very dissatisfied with the behaviour of some of the top people in the police stations. This led to a certain passivity on their part and dissatisfaction. As soon as the war broke out, many joined the military precisely because they did not agree with that type of work that was being introduced in practice as the system was crumbling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further on when answering the Prosecutor's question, this is now another tape, it is marked T-002554 until 2554 [as interpreted] page 14 of the transcript. The Prosecutor asked you how often you met with Mr. Zupljanin, and you said that it was roughly once in 1992 and then perhaps twice a month. It depended on whether there was any need for you to meet up. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I did speak about that topic, but I really cannot remember how many times we had met up really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your interview, you mentioned a few of these meetings that you had recalled so my questions will be related to those meetings. One of the topics that you discussed with the Prosecutor and that is related to Mr. Zupljanin was the question of this group of Veljko Milankovic's, the so-called wolves from Vucjak. Do you remember that unit that was creating problems in that zone, if we can put it that way, between the CSB Doboj and the CSB Banja Luka, that area between the two?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember one particular thing that happened. The commander of the barracks in Doboj came from the direction of Banja Luka, Colonel Cazim Hadzic, they stopped him, we have already mentioned him here. They checked him and when they came back Colonel Cazim told us about this, and we established, judging by the location involved, that on that day, that is to say, when they were carrying out these checks they were in the municipality of Prnjavor. They were not in the territory of the area of the CSB Doboj. At the time I informed Mr. Zupljanin about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said to the Prosecutor further on in this interview that you know that this group of Veljko Milankovic's was arrested right after that happened; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot remember the exact day that this happened, but indeed that group together with their commander Milankovic was arrested. I remember that. That was done by the milicija that was at the time in the area of the CSB Banja Luka because they had authority there in terms of territory. Veljko Milankovic and his people were based there around Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document now because in your interview you said that you weren't sure whether it was the military or the police that had originally arrested Milankovic. Could the witness please be shown 2D0073. Number 2, tab number 2 in the Stojan Zupljanin Defence. I'm going to show you a document briefly. This is the Milankovic that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was born in Kremna near Prnjavor, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And we see this decision on his arrest and someone signed on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin. Sorry, your answer was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recognise that. It was that Veljko Milankovic who led the wolves from Vucjak and Kremna is his native village and he lived there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, when answering the Prosecutor's questions you said -- well, but that was in 2009 in your interview then, that is page 24, T-001-1856. I think you mentioned something during your testimony, actually in May 1992 a number of the employees of the state security sector came from Banja Luka to Doboj to help out; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a number of operatives came who worked with the people from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I didn't turn on my microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When answering the Prosecutor's question then, you said that to the best of your knowledge, this had been agreed upon between Dusan Zivkovic, the head of the state security in Doboj, and Kesic, the head of state security in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the two of them as the chiefs of that service had agreed upon that, that is my assumption. I don't know how else these people could have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you then whether you knew that a number of people came then from the unit of Special Police from Banja Luka, and your answer then was that a small number of people came who were providing security for these operatives; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly how many of them came but indeed it was a small number, that is what I observed. I think that they took turns but on the whole there wasn't more than 15 of them involving all shifts, that is my estimate. Since we are talking about those people now, on one occasion one of them addressed me and said that he had certain knowledge since he was in this building where the police and the state security service were, that I was facing some kind of danger and that I should take care of my own safety and security. I remember that one of them said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge and that is what you said on page 26 of your interview, that's to say the next page, these people were not securing any specific buildings in Doboj and they were not involved in any other kind of police work. They were only securing this group of state security operatives; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm going to show you a document now. This is in Prosecutor tab 96, 2D89 MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in on the top part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is a reference to the 9th Company for special assignments, Banja Luka, and there's a list of some 15 persons on that list. This roughly corresponds to what you had said, that there was a total of 15 of them in two shifts, so not all 15 of them were there at the same time. They took turns; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they took turns. I can't remember whether there were two or three shifts involved, but I know that they were not there at the same time all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now please be shown --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, before we do that, this document was MFI'd at the time and this witness has identified it, so I wonder if we could have the MFI removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a problem with this document. Actually, it cannot be translated. We sent it out for translation twice and the translation service said that it cannot be translated. Since the Prosecutor was opposed to having it admitted, then I left it at that so I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are quite happy for it to be de-MFI'd. I agree it's very difficult to read and that's the problem, but certainly we may as well have it properly exhibited even without a full translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that the translation is not accurate. That's my only comment. So I really have no position on this. The translation that came back from the CLSS is not accurate. That's the essence of what I'm saying. But we have the testimony of this witness and other witnesses, so I think it shouldn't be terribly important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can't go on having a document referred to as often as this one without it having exhibited. We'll see what we can do about a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we are going to have to return to the question of whether the MFI qualification should be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P1340, tab 90 Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 90?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 90. During the examination of Mr. Zecevic, he showed you this document and you explained for which purpose it was drafted. If I understood you correctly, you requested the chief of the public security station in Doboj to submit a report about all stolen vehicles including all the details about who was driving them at the time and where, and all this because there were complaints from citizens in relation to unlawful appropriation of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this part people from Banja Luka told you that it was known that only one vehicle was used by a person from Mr. Banja Luka, while other vehicles were related to other people and not to the members of this unit; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We dealt with this problem. We attempted to collect as much information as possible, to find out what exactly happened with those vehicles, what were the registration numbers, where they are, and we managed to find out that, yes, one among the people from Banja Luka did take away a vehicle. I think it was Jetta as far as I can remember, although I see here they say it was a Passat, now I don't quite remember exactly what it was, but as for the other vehicles it wasn't found out that they were taken by those persons and that they were taken towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Renault 5 that was allegedly taken by the Special Police from Banja Luka, it turned out that it was taken away by Slobodan Karagic, and you told us that he also testified in this case, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a trial in Doboj in relation to that vehicle. Karagic claimed that the vehicle was mobilised and that's why I was called as a witness. The vehicle had not been mobilised. At the time there was a practice, and I think that I had informed the minister at the collegium meetings about it. Vehicles would be driven around with the registration plates covered. Very often they would say that those vehicles were mobilized vehicle, well, actually, they were not. The lawful procedure had not been followed. It was basically a case of theft and I think the same goes for this Renault 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document you never had a conversation with Mr. Zupljanin about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in addition to this unit, the unit that was securing the operatives that came from the state security, was there any other special reconnaissance unit in Doboj comprised from people -- comprised by people from Banja Luka in May or June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time especially in June there was a number of units from the area of Krajina because of the combat operations that were going on. I would like to use this opportunity to emphasise one thing. You reminded me now of an event. I testified here about the problem that I had when on one occasion people stopped me and they were carrying rifles. At that time I had some documents relating to information about the enemy forces. After that incident, I took those documents and went to the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps. When I arrived there, General Talic noticed simply by observing me that something had happened. He asked me what had happened. I really wanted to avoid talking about that because it was unpleasant for me. It was a very unpleasant experience. However, General Talic insisted. He saw that I did not behave in the way that I had behaved when I left him. He asked me whether somebody was killed from my family. And then I told him what happened and he said, ah, things are not going to go on like that. Since I didn't have any security people who would take care of me, I told him that I only had a driver. He said that he would give me protection. And for awhile he gave me, I think it was a reconnaissance unit, their commander was Zoran. I think there were about 10 or 12 of them, and later when I arrived to the police building, they entered the building and secured it, meaning that they he secured the entrance, the staircase, my office on the first floor, and for awhile they performed the function of my security. And then as a reaction to that, the Predini Vukovi unit arrived and they wanted to have a shoot-out with the unit that was securing me. I sought a compromise and from that point on there was nobody there. Neither those chaps from the corps command. We somehow managed to avoid an incident and a shoot-out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This unit from the corps command, they were from Banja Luka, they dressed in a different way and they had undergone a different training from regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The way I understood it, I think they were some sort of reconnaissance unit. They were the unit in charge of the security of the command at the forward command post. I think they were engaged in some other activities as well. I think that they were reconnaissance activities. They were very able people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of berets they had, or whether they had any berets, this unit from Banja Luka that you were describing a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly, they had different caps. They changed them. They didn't wear the same caps all the time. Sometimes they had berets, sometimes they had camouflage hats. Because that unit spent quite some time around the command, so they did not have the same caps all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I have another question. In response to the questions by the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just one moment. Mr. Bjelosevic, just a moment ago when we talked about a unit changing berets, were we talking now about the unit that secured you or were we talking about what's the name, the Predini Vukovi unit? I'm little bit confused here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Predini Vukovi also used to change their uniform and the caps, but in answering the question of Mr. Krgovic, I was talking about the unit attached to the corps command and about the people who were my security for a while. I think that sometimes they wore berets, and if I remember it correctly, sometimes they had camouflage hats, just as they had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip the chronology now. I want to talk about the meeting that you discussed with Mr. Zecevic. It was the meeting in Belgrade on the 11th of July. It's page 12 of the interview, tape T-0002559, 2004. Mr. Bjelosevic, you remember, you were present at that meeting on the 11th of July in Belgrade. It's Stanisic Defence tab 66. P160.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor about the meeting and its participants. Can you turn to page 8. Actually, that's the page in e-court, and in your binder it should be page 4. It's marked. In English it's also page 8 in e-court. P160. Maybe I wrote it down incorrectly. 66, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 8 in e-court both in Serbian and English. And in your binder it begins on the fourth page and goes over to the fifth page. ERN number is 0324-1855. Excuse me, Mr. Bjelosevic, it seems that we have a problem with e-court so we are waiting for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P160, tab 66, I apologise. I wasn't precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you recall that you spoke about this with the Prosecutor. Mr. Zupljanin says here, I will paraphrase, that the military and the Crisis Staff or War Presidencies should collect the Muslim population, that they are collecting them into such undefined centres, and then handing them over to the workers of the interior. And you commented on this, if you remember that. Do you remember that Mr. Zupljanin spoke about these events?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that he mentioned it during his discussion. I also remember the interview with the investigator, and I remember him asking me about Mr. Zupljanin's discussion. If I recall it correctly, I think that he asked me what did Zupljanin have in mind when he was saying that. It's very hard for me to know what he had in mind, but obviously if he highlighted it as a problem, it means that he doesn't agree with what was going on. That's the only understanding that I could have about the reasons that he spoke about what he spoke. He highlighted this as a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said that that was a problem and that you had the impression based on Zupljanin's words that Zupljanin thought that this was inappropriate, that things were not supposed to be done in such a way, that he complained about it, and according to your understanding, the manner that he spoke about it meant that he requested assistance from the ministry in order that something be done about it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the general direction of the discussion. He highlighted this as a problem and he requested assistance from the ministry so that the problem could begin to be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you remember that in the conclusions from the meeting it was also decided that the highest leadership of Republika Srpska should be apprised of the problem so that it could be solved?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have the conclusions here and it is beyond dispute that that was highlighted as a problem be and that it formed a part of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is an appropriate moment to break. Thank you Mr. Bjelosevic, for today, we are going to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to resume tomorrow morning at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention one matter. Mr. Krgovic filed a motion supporting Stanisic's motion which you dismissed yesterday, therefore we don't propose to take any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's appears too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
